We have exactly 8 hours maximum to build a fully functional prototype. We are shooting to achieve this functional POC in half that time to leave the remaining half for polish work. It is of utmost important to minimize wall clock time during this hackathon, to do that we must be cognizant of which models and thinking levels we choose to execute with as well as how much context window we allow them to operate on. We should optimize for total time, not individual task time. It is better to take 15 minutes to do it right the first time than spend 10 minutes doing it wrong and then another 10 minutes correcting it.

We are building a POC from complete scratch and it should be deployable as a single docker container that we can deploy and run anywhere. You are executing in a windows environment with an Ubuntu WSL subsystem. Make full use of this, we will eventually be deploying the docker container to a ubuntu VPS for judging. This POC is POC scope. All features that add time and aren't explicitly called for should be left on the cutting floor. Be judiciuos about trimming scope.

Due to the time limite we should operate on iterative release cycles to prove a functionality complete before moving on to the next set.

We are being judged on our ability to execute well and have a polished project at the end, even if it is minimal, one feature delivered well is bettern than dozen half baked ideas.

We are being judged on our depth of knowledge and creativity. We both have that in spades here, make sure we're using both of our heads to the best of our ability.

Context As AI capabilities advance rapidly, engineers at [company] face a unique challenge: building tools and experiences that are genuinely useful, trustworthy, and delightful. The best products demonstrate taste, handle complexity gracefully, and solve real problems in non-obvious ways. This assignment asks you to build something that showcases your judgment, creativity, and execution.

Objective Build a functional prototype that demonstrates your ability to ship an impressive, self-contained experience. Choose one of the following themes: Theme 1: Exploration & Understanding Complex systems, technical concepts, and unfamiliar artifacts are hard to understand through static explanation. Build a tool that helps users develop deepunderstanding—whether that's a simulation of emergent dynamics, an explainer for a technical concept, or a tool for exploring codebases, datasets, or documents

I'm an expert in astrophotography and often spend a lot of time explaining to beginners about stacking images in astrophotography. Beginners often ask questions about the required calibration images, how many light images to select, how to stack, what algorithms to use, etc. Stacking images for astrophotography is all about applied mathmatics, mostly statistics, and understanding the electrical properties of image acquision, signal to noise and management of outliers.

We want to build an explainer with a sample dataset from my observatory to teach beginners in a very easy to understand process that is interactive and preconfigured that gives them the tools and instructions to delightfully pick and chose images to produce the highest SNR stacked image. It must be interactive, with tight feedback loops so that they may understand in real time how their choices affect the final result. The best way to teach is by doing. We want to help them understand what they should select to produce the best final image, but we don't want to force their hand, let them select bad options and flip back to good options to see the real impact on the final result.

We shall use sample images from ./source_images for our demonstration. * ./source_images/light contain the raw xisf images from the night's capture * ./source_images/light_registered contains xisf images that have underwent star alignment and have metadata to align their pixel grids. * ./source_images/light_synthetic_disaster contains fits images that are identical to the lights except they've been modified to introduce synthetic errors. Frame 11 has a synthetic tracking error resulting in elongated stars, and frame 14-16 have synthetic cloud cover. These will have the same registration and pixel mapping as their unmodified sources, but they themselves have not been through registration. Any time these are used, use the aligment from their untouched relatives. * ./source_images/calibration includes possible calibration frames to use, there is a mastered bias and dark image here. Additionally there are several sets of flats from a flat panel and the corresponding dark flats. These flats are 10% histogram saturation, 50% and 85%. There is also a dark master from an older camera to show amp glow. * ./source_images/final has two samples of my work to prove what is possible with the dataset. One is the mastered red image and the other is a final composit color image.

We have two main goals: * Explaining how to select calibration images * Explaining how to select light images

We want to explain the relationship between read noise, sensor noise and environmental factors like dust on a sensor. Right now, the calibration folder contains a bias image, a dark image and a flat image at 50% histogram. Those are all best practices. We need to explain to the user, preferably with SVGs what comprises the noise of a light image and how each calibration frame removes it. Deepskystacker has a great explainer on the types of calibration images. Our SVG explainers should represent color coded layers being peeled away. Review the actual source images to generate overly simplifed representations. These SVGs should show the system (telescope -> camera -> sensor -> sensor PCB with op-amp and a2d chips).

Bias images are images that are taken as quickly as the sensor can be read, in complete darkness. This gives us a picture comprised of mostly the baseline noise of the sensor that is generated during reading the actual chip. Dark images are images that are taken at the same exposure time as the light images and the same temperature. This gives us the noise of the sensor that is produced during long exposures. This noise is temperature dependant, so using darks that are taken at the same temperature as the exposures are paramount. This and the bias images can also give us an idea of hot and cold pixels on the sensor. In this example, the dark calibration image is currently constructed at a slightly different temperature than the lights. This is acceptable, use this. Flat images are images that are evenly illuminated and give us an idea of the noise from the environment, from dust and fingerprints on the sensor, telescope or filters, to vigenetting of the sensor. These are not temperature dependant nor time dependant as long as they don't approach bias images in speed since we want the primarly output of these images to be not read noise, but environmental noise. A second or more is perfect. Even exposure is important, as we progress on this hackathon we will consider adding other types of flats to experiment with: over and under exposed flats and sky flats. Dark flats. a dark flat is a flat image, just like the flats that are for the evenly illuminated, but taken in the dark. So match the exposure time of the flats but do it without illumination. In this example, a dark flat is provided with an exposure time nearly identical to the flats.

This is where the fun starts. We want to teach the user about the relationship between noise, exposure time, and exposure count. Then we want to teach them about stacking algorithms.

Stacking algorithms to offer: * Average * Median * kappa-sigma clipping * winsorized sigma clipping * robust chauvenet rejection

We want to explain the difference between the algorithms, how the treat outliers and how the determine what is an outlier. There is an image in this dataset with a sattelite trail. We should highight it's effects on stacking.

Throughout all of this we want to show the user a reference image of their selection (default to to the first image) and then select up to 4 ROI points that we'll auto update after changing their stacking options. We will set the size of the ROI and provide default placements, one over the place where the satelite trail is in frame 3, one over the central galaxy including nebulosity, not just the core, one over the cluster of galaxies just above the central galaxy, and a final one over the dust mote on the left hand side of the image.

* All processing should be done in javascript on the user's computer, we'll have no backend. We should only process the ROI sections until the user askes for the full image processing. Stacking the full image is likely to take 4-10 seconds, but we can do each of the ROI sections in under a second. * Users should select/deselect calibration frames first * All images should be stretched for easy viewing for the user. Use a consistent stretch based on the selected reference frame. Calibration images get their own individual stretch and do not need a reference selection. Flats should not be stretched. * Changing reference frame changes the displayed reference frame where the four ROI's are positioned. * ROI positions are fixed and the user may not change them. * This is a single page app with no authentication, caching (outside of one specific usecase), or other non-hackathon style features. Navigating in the single page app should not prevent the browser back button from functioning. * For the workbench - The exported image after complete stacking should be a fits file or png depending on user selection. - We should provide a list of buttons at the top for preconfigured scenarios: + Default: All frames that don't have a synthetic problem introduced are selected and median pixel value is selected. + Naive: Where all images are selected for stacking regardless of quality. + Satelite Trial Challenge: Where we select only a few images plus the image with the satelite trail and pixel averaging algorithm and allow the user to experiment with ways to make the satellite trail disappear without losing the rest of the signal in the image. + Cloud Challenge: Where we select the images with clouds disrupting the view and two other high quality images + Tracking error challenge: Where we select the image with a tracking error and two other high quality images. - Along with the list of images to chose from, we should display the image histogram, FWHM and star detection counts. We'll hardcode these to prevent having to calucate them on each test. * Since we're allowing the user to chose from any or none of the calibration images, we should precompute a master each permutation of flats: with/without bias, dark or dark flats. * Since the computation time for some of these images can be extreme, we should store any computed image in localstorage with the exact combination that led to it's computation. This will allow the users to quickly flip back and forth between settings. This cache should be purged on page refresh.

We will follow the Park Tool's how to repair instruction style. We'll explain a concept in breif, introduce a problem, and let the user articulate it until the problem goes away, and to demonstrate mastery they can reintroduce the problem and solve it again (if desired).

We are teaching people with very little knowledge of astrophotography, we should avoid unnessecary details and asides that will distract, confuse or overwhelm the user. For example, instead of saying "ADU" we'll reference "pixel brightness", instead of saying "matched darks" we'll say "dark images with the same exposure time as X". Short pithy declaritive statements are to be avoided. Our prose should strike a balance between textbook style and an impassioned expert excited to share their knowledge with a beginner. When we write the prose in figma, expect signficant editing from me.

We will design this website as a wizard/lesson with multiple steps. Each step will contain an interactive element for the user to learn about. Think interactive infographic. Once the user has completed the lesson we'll drop them into a workbench where they may tweak and experiment as much as they'd like to master their own red filter image. The pages we'll be designing will be: * Welcome page - This will demonstrate what is possible and show single frame -> mastered image -> final image, this is our emotional hook to get them excited. We'll stress that these are real images from my backyard observatory (Stella Venator Observatory) in Lexington Kentucky. * Noise & Defects - This page will set the groundwork in breif for the lessons to come. We'll explain in breif the sources of noise and explain why we stack images. Noise sources come from random variations, bias, dark signal, uneven response in the sensor (i.e. flats), as well as other non-hardware noise like tracking errors, clouds, airplanes and satelites, etc. We'll explain what we mean by calibration frames * Calibration - This page is about how to construct all the calibration images and what each type is. This will be subdivided into 4 subpages - Bias - Darks - Flats (what flats do, demonstration of flats and dark flats) - Flats - Continued (histogram targets for flats and why it's important, might have an asside about mean well depth of the sensor, but I may judge it to be too confusing to the user) * Alignment - This page will explain how we bring more than one photo together, how it affects SNR and how images are registered. Importantly registration is already done in the sample images, but we can demonstrate it by stacking naively a set of 2 images with averaging and showing the doubling of data. We should select images with the biggest alignment offset excluding meridian flips. Then show them how it's done by highlighting a trio of stars used for alignment and averaging those same two images together. Importantly this is the first time the user can see the changes in detail, make them look at the background. * Algorithms - This page will describe the algorithms avaliable, what makes them different from each other and when and how to use them (i.e., frame count ranges). We'll use the sattelite trail as an example of something that can be managed by image selection, offer a stack of 5 images, one averaging, one doing median. We'll want to explain the algorithms from a high school math understanding. Knowledge of algebra and basic calc, but not stats understanding. Saying sigma will glaze over most folks eyes, but standard deviation might make more sense. * Light Frames - This is the page where we'll teach them how to select images and sources of noise that we can't eliminate with calibration frames, such as clouds, tracking errors, etc. We'll want to explain how to select for high quality images, talk about FWHM, but make sure that the user knows that those are only tools, judgement is critical. The experiment here will be a light version of the workbench, we'll show them all the images they can select from, and offer them average or median stacking options, instruct them to flip through the images and build the best image. We'll show one ROI on the bigger galaxy. Tease them with the other algorithms in the workbench. We'll high it from them, but here we'll be applying all the calibration frames for them. * Workbench - This is where they get to do everything. We'll design this page collaboratively.

We'll design for a 1 or 2 column layout, fixed width, unbounded height. We'll use bauhaus philosophy for the layout and colors. We'll space theme it, but not target an overly dark theme. We'll use tailwind We're designing for desktop only. No mobile. Accessibility is out of scope for a hackathon.

1. Spec development and precomputing data - We'll collabroative define the spec for this project and all features, determine story plan and execution. Spec will include defining the orchestration/agent workflow for fully autonomous implementation and validation. - A background agent will precompute the required data for this project: The masters, the PSF, FWHM. 2. Figma design, I have created a blank figma design here: https://www.figma.com/design/2qUdD8ENFca1ZMCS4aiTUf/Stacking-Explainer-2?m=dev&t=wZ9HAQ6QNXFNFLPu-1 we'll iterate on this until we're both happy with the design. - We should design with the idea of infographich type display. We're trying to teach and easily accessible design is helpful here. - Before we dive into the design, let's put our helds together and talk about the design philosphy, style and goals. I have lots of input here. 3. Quick re-evaluation of the story plan and spec following the figma design. Any stories need to be added or removed from the spec? Did the figma design turn up new features? Eliminate features? Surface features we forgot? 4. Milestone 1: We'll implement the display and selection of all images and calibration images. - ROI sections will be placeholders taken from the reference image - We'll be able to click through and see all the calibration images and light images along with their applied stretch - All UI elements will be present on the display, even if only placeholders. 5. Milestone 2: Stacking with pixel averaging and median - We can click the button to be presented with the stacked final image using pixel averaging. Null values on edges should not be counted, the resulting image will not be autocropped. - ROI samples will auto update as we change image selections - Calibration images will be applied in the correct order. 6. Milestone 3: Lesson construction - We'll make all lessons able to be articulated by the end user. 7. Milesone 4: Stacking with all pixel combination algos + scenarios - We can select all stacking algorithms and see the changes in the resulting ROI options and final calibrated image - All scenarios are functional.

Review this plan, and restate our plan. Ask any questions you need to and then let's proceed to planning.

---
name: astro-image
description: Convert, stretch, measure and denoise astrophotography images (FITS/XISF) with the project CLI tools/astro.py. Use when producing web assets (PNG 8/16-bit, JPEG, WebP) from FITS or XISF, applying a PixInsight-style auto STF stretch, detecting stars and measuring FWHM/eccentricity, or starlet-wavelet denoising / visualizing wavelet layers.
---

# astro-image

Run everything via `uv run tools/astro.py <cmd>` from the repo root. The first `uv sync` creates `.venv`. Add `--help` to any command for the full options.

## Pick the command
- **Web image from raw data:** `convert in.fits out.jpg --stretch --quality 85`. For a lossless version use `out.png --bits 16`. Leave out `--stretch` when you want linear data. Linear data looks almost black, which is itself a teaching point.
- **Stretch only:** `stretch in.xisf out.png`. This is PixInsight AutoSTF: target background 0.25, shadows clip −2.8·MADN, channels linked. Use `--unlinked` to neutralize a colour cast. `--shadows/--midtones` set a manual STF. The parameters used are printed to stderr as JSON, so record them if the page shows them.
- **Star metrics:** `stars in.fits [--model moffat] [--pixscale 1.94] --csv s.csv --overlay s.png`. Run it **only on linear, unstretched** data. Stretching changes star profiles. The FWHM guess iterates automatically; pass `--fwhm-guess` to pin it. Output is JSON on stdout with `n_stars`, `fwhm_px_median`, `fwhm_arcsec_median`, `ecc_median`, `background` and `noise`.
- **Denoise:** `denoise in.fits out.xisf --layers 1:3:1,2:2:0.8 --n-layers 4`. Each entry is `layer:threshold(σ):amount`. `--dump-layers DIR` writes each starlet scale as a PNG for diagrams. Add `--stretch` when the output is .png/.jpg.
- **One-shot-colour CFA subs:** add `--debayer auto` (reads BAYERPAT) or `--debayer RGGB`. This is a 2×2 superpixel debayer, so the image comes out at half resolution.
- **Inspect:** `info in.fits` prints the key headers (IMAGETYP, EXPTIME, GAIN, CCD-TEMP, BAYERPAT…), median/MADN and arcsec/px.

## Rules
- Raw inputs live in `source_images/` (git-ignored; see AGENTS.md › Data layout). Write committed web assets only via a recorded command, so they can be regenerated.
- After changing `tools/astro.py`, run `uv run pytest tools`. The tests use synthetic frames with a known FWHM (3.5 px) and known noise.
- In Python you can `import astro` (add `tools/` to `sys.path`) for `load`, `save`, `auto_stf`, `apply_stf`, `mtf`, `measure_stars`, `starlet` and `denoise`. That's handy for composite figures such as histograms before and after a stretch.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Astro image helpers for producing the explainer's assets.

Run with `uv run tools/astro.py <command> --help`. Commands:
  info     header and pixel statistics
  convert  FITS/XISF -> PNG (8/16-bit), JPEG, WebP, FITS or XISF, optionally stretched
  stretch  PixInsight-style auto STF (or manual shadows/midtones), then save
  stars    detect stars on a linear image and measure FWHM (elliptical Gaussian or Moffat fits)
  denoise  starlet (a trous B3-spline) wavelet denoise on chosen layers

Internally every image is float32, shape (C, H, W), normalized to [0, 1].
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- I/O

HEADER_KEYS = ("IMAGETYP", "FRAME", "EXPTIME", "EXPOSURE", "GAIN", "OFFSET", "CCD-TEMP", "SET-TEMP",
               "BAYERPAT", "XBINNING", "XPIXSZ", "FOCALLEN", "FILTER", "OBJECT", "INSTRUME", "TELESCOP", "DATE-OBS")


def _normalize(data: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Map integer data to [0,1] by dtype range; float data is kept if already in [0,1]."""
    if np.issubdtype(data.dtype, np.integer):
        info = np.iinfo(data.dtype)
        return ((data.astype(np.float64) - info.min) / (info.max - info.min)).astype(np.float32)
    data = data.astype(np.float32)
    hi = float(np.nanmax(data))
    if hi > 1.0:  # float ADU (e.g. calibrated FITS from other software)
        data = data / (65535.0 if hi <= 65535.0 else hi)
    return np.nan_to_num(np.clip(data, 0.0, 1.0))


def load(path: str | Path) -> tuple[np.ndarray, dict]:
    """Return (image[C,H,W] float32 in [0,1], header dict)."""
    path = Path(path)
    ext = path.suffix.lower()
    if ext in (".fits", ".fit", ".fts"):
        from astropy.io import fits
        with fits.open(path) as hdul:
            hdu = next(h for h in hdul if h.data is not None)
            data = hdu.data
            header = {k: hdu.header[k] for k in hdu.header if k and k not in ("COMMENT", "HISTORY")}
        # astropy applies BZERO/BSCALE; unsigned 16-bit comes back as uint16
        if data.ndim == 2:
            data = data[None]
    elif ext == ".xisf":
        from xisf import XISF
        meta: dict = {}
        data = XISF.read(str(path), image_metadata=meta)  # (H, W, C)
        data = np.moveaxis(data, -1, 0)
        header = {k: v[0]["value"] for k, v in meta.get("FITSKeywords", {}).items() if v}
    else:
        raise SystemExit(f"unsupported input: {path}")
    return _normalize(np.ascontiguousarray(data)), header


def debayer_superpixel(img: np.ndarray, pattern: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """2x2 superpixel debayer of a single-channel CFA frame (halves resolution, no interpolation)."""
    pattern = pattern.upper()
    cfa = img[0]
    h, w = cfa.shape[0] // 2 * 2, cfa.shape[1] // 2 * 2
    planes = [cfa[0:h:2, 0:w:2], cfa[0:h:2, 1:w:2], cfa[1:h:2, 0:w:2], cfa[1:h:2, 1:w:2]]
    by = {"R": [], "G": [], "B": []}
    for ch, plane in zip(pattern, planes):
        by[ch].append(plane)
    return np.stack([np.mean(by[c], axis=0) for c in "RGB"]).astype(np.float32)


def save(img: np.ndarray, path: str | Path, bits: int = 8, quality: int = 90, header: dict | None = None) -> None:
    """Save (C,H,W) [0,1] image. Format from extension: .png (8/16-bit), .jpg/.jpeg, .webp, .fits, .xisf."""
    path = Path(path)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    ext = path.suffix.lower()

$ Bash
Dump headers and alignment matrices for all frames
mkdir -p /tmp/claude-1000/-mnt-c-Users-Jerome-Hollon-Documents-claude-astrophotography-explainer/33479da6-dcd1-4ed0-a9ea-71a5ec470ddd/scratchpad && cat > /tmp/claude-1000/-mnt-c-Users-Jerome-Hollon-Documents-claude-astrophotography-explainer/33479da6-dcd1-4ed0-a9ea-71a5ec470ddd/scratchpad/hdr.py <<'EOF'
import struct, re, glob, math, os, sys
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from astropy.io import fits
KEYS=("IMAGETYP","EXPTIME","EXPOSURE","GAIN","OFFSET","CCD-TEMP","SET-TEMP","DATE-OBS","PIERSIDE","XBINNING","NAXIS1","NAXIS2","BITPIX","INSTRUME","CAMERA","FOCALLEN","XPIXSZ","OBJCTROT","ROTATOR","ROTANG","AIRMASS","CENTALT")
def xisf_hdr(p):
    with open(p,'rb') as f:
        sig=f.read(8); n=struct.unpack('<I',f.read(4))[0]; f.read(4); x=f.read(n).decode('utf8','replace')
    kw={}
    for m in re.finditer(r'<FITSKeyword name="([^"]+)" value="([^"]*)"',x): kw.setdefault(m.group(1),m.group(2).strip("' "))
    img=re.search(r'<Image [^>]*>',x).group(0)
    props=re.findall(r'<Property id="([^"]+)"[^>]*?(?:value="([^"]*)")?',x)
    return kw,img,props,x
def show(p):
    if p.endswith('.xisf'):
        kw,img,props,x=xisf_hdr(p)
        geo=re.search(r'geometry="([^"]+)"',img).group(1); fmt=re.search(r'sampleFormat="([^"]+)"',img).group(1)
        comp=re.search(r'compression="([^"]+)"',img); 
        print(os.path.basename(p)[:70], geo, fmt, comp.group(1) if comp else '', {k:kw[k] for k in KEYS if k in kw})
        return kw,props,x
    else:
        h=fits.getheader(p)
        print(os.path.basename(p)[:70], {k:h[k] for k in KEYS if k in h})
        return h,None,None
S='source_images/'
print("== lights"); 
for p in sorted(glob.glob(S+'light/*.xisf')): show(p)
print("== synthetic"); 
for p in sorted(glob.glob(S+'light_synthetic_disaster/*')): show(p)
print("== calib")
for p in sorted(glob.glob(S+'calibration/*')):
    if os.path.isfile(p):
        r=show(p)
for d in sorted(glob.glob(S+'calibration/raw flats/*/*')):
    fs=sorted(glob.glob(d+'/**/*.xisf',recursive=True)); print('--',d, len(fs)); show(fs[0])
print("== final"); 
kw,props,x=show(glob.glob(S+'final/*.xisf')[0])
print("== registered sample")
kw,props,x=show(sorted(glob.glob(S+'light_registered/*.xisf'))[0])
print([p[0] for p in props][:60])
print(re.findall(r'HISTORY[^/]*',x)[:20])
print("== alignment")
for p in sorted(glob.glob(S+'light_registered/*.xdrz')):
    t=open(p).read(); m=[float(v) for v in re.search(r'<AlignmentMatrix>([^<]+)',t).group(1).split(',')]
    rot=math.degrees(math.atan2(m[3],m[0])); sc=math.hypot(m[0],m[3])
    fr=re.search(r'FRAME_(\d+)',p).group(1)
    extra='SPLINE' if 'Spline' in t else ''
    print(fr, f"dx={m[2]:9.2f} dy={m[5]:9.2f} rot={rot:8.3f} scale={sc:.5f} persp=({m[6]:.1e},{m[7]:.1e})", extra)
EOF

import sys, glob, re, struct, numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0,'tools'); import astro
S='source_images/'
def bin4(a): h,w=a.shape[0]//4*4,a.shape[1]//4*4; return a[:h,:w].reshape(h//4,4,w//4,4).mean((1,3))
def hp(b):  # high-pass-ish normalize so correlation keys on stars
    from scipy.ndimage import uniform_filter
    d=b-uniform_filter(b,25); return (d-d.mean())/d.std()
def ncc(a,b): return float((hp(a)*hp(b)).mean())
# rotator values
for p in sorted(glob.glob(S+'light/*.xisf'))[::4]+sorted(glob.glob(S+'calibration/raw flats/*/*/*.xisf')+glob.glob(S+'calibration/raw flats/*/*/*/*.xisf'))[::25]:
    with open(p,'rb') as f:

    reg=bin4(astro.load(glob.glob(S+f'light_registered/*FRAME_{fr}*.xisf')[0])[0][0])

import sys, glob, numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import median_filter, maximum_filter
sys.path.insert(0,'tools'); import astro
S='source_images/'
def bin4(a): h,w=a.shape[0]//4*4,a.shape[1]//4*4; return a[:h,:w].reshape(h//4,4,w//4,4).mean((1,3))
def top(a,n=6):
    b=median_filter(bin4(a),3); m=(b==maximum_filter(b,40))
    ys,xs=np.nonzero(m); v=b[ys,xs]; o=np.argsort(v)[::-1][:n]
    return [(int(xs[i]*4),int(ys[i]*4)) for i in o]
for fr in ('0003','0007','0011','0014'):
    raw=astro.load(glob.glob(S+f'light/*FRAME_{fr}*.xisf')[0])[0][0]
    print(fr,'raw ',top(raw))
    s=glob.glob(S+f'light_synthetic_disaster/*{fr}*')
    if s:
        syn=astro.load(s[0])[0][0]; print(fr,'syn ',top(syn))
        print(fr,'exact-equal pixel fraction syn==raw', float((np.abs(syn-raw)<1e-7).mean()), ' syn==rot180(raw)', float((np.abs(syn-raw[::-1,::-1])<1e-7).mean()))
    reg=astro.load(glob.glob(S+f'light_registered/*FRAME_{fr}*.xisf')[0])[0][0]; print(fr,'reg ',top(reg))
EOF

import sys, glob, numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0,'tools'); import astro
from PIL import Image
S='source_images/'; OUT='/tmp/claude-1000/-mnt-c-Users-Jerome-Hollon-Documents-claude-astrophotography-explainer/33479da6-dcd1-4ed0-a9ea-71a5ec470ddd/scratchpad/'
Y0,Y1,X0,X1=2100,2800,350,1050
def crops(pattern,n=9):
    fs=sorted(glob.glob(pattern))[:n]; out=[];meds=[]
    for f in fs:
        a=astro.load(f)[0][0]; out.append(a[Y0:Y1,X0:X1].copy()); meds.append(float(np.median(a[1500:2700,2500:3700])))
    return np.median(out,0), np.median(meds)
D=astro.load(S+'calibration/masterDark_BIN-1_6224x4168_EXPOSURE-300.00s.xisf')[0][0][Y0:Y1,X0:X1]
L=astro.load(glob.glob(S+'light/*FRAME_0003*.xisf')[0])[0][0][Y0:Y1,X0:X1]
res={}
for name,fl,dk in [('50',S+'calibration/raw flats/50% histogram/flat/*.xisf',S+'calibration/raw flats/50% histogram/dark/*.xisf'),
                   ('10',S+'calibration/raw flats/10% histogram/FLAT/Red/*.xisf',S+'calibration/raw flats/10% histogram/DARK/Red/*.xisf'),
                   ('85',S+'calibration/raw flats/85% histogram/FLAT/Red/*.xisf',S+'calibration/raw flats/85% histogram/DARK/Red/*.xisf')]:
    F,fm=crops(fl); DF,dm=crops(dk)
    Fn=(F-DF)/(fm-dm)
    C=(L-D)/Fn
    res[name]=C
    print(name,'flat centre level',round(fm*65535),'darkflat',round(dm*65535),'flat min/max in crop',round(float(Fn.min()),3),round(float(Fn.max()),3))
raw=L-D
def row(img):
    p=astro.auto_stf(img[None]); return np.clip(astro.apply_stf(img[None],p)[0],0,1)
tiles=[row(raw)]+[row(res[k]) for k in ('10','50','85')]
im=np.concatenate([t[::2,::2] for t in tiles],1)
Image.fromarray((im*255).astype(np.uint8)).save(OUT+'flatchk.jpg',quality=88)
EOF

Found 2026-09-24 during the hackathon kickoff (8-hour POC, stacking explainer):

- `light_registered/*_r.xisf` are registered but NOT calibrated (UInt16 raw). Calibration must happen in sensor space before warping.
- `.xdrz` AlignmentMatrix is a 3x3 homography mapping reference coords -> raw frame coords (pixel-centre origin 0.5). Reference frame is FRAME_0007 (identity).
- Frames 0-7 PIERSIDE West, 8-19 East (~180° rotation). Largest same-side offset: frames 2/3 vs 5 (~47 px).
- Synthetic FITS in `light_synthetic_disaster/` are vertically flipped (FITS bottom-up rows) relative to raw XISF. flipud before applying the untouched relative's matrix.
- Frame 11 synthetic = tracking error (trailed stars); frame 3 has a real faint satellite trail (lower-right); 14-16 synthetic clouds.
- Master dark median ~161 vs master bias ~160.5, so the dark includes bias and dark current is negligible.
- darkFromOlderCamera.fits is an ASI294MM Pro, 8288x5644, 600 s, gain 120. Different sensor size.
- Quick test: the 50% flat removes the left-side dust mote (~sensor x700,y2400); the 85% flat leaves it visible.

Related: [[planning-means-planning]]

You're right. You asked me to review the plan and I went off inspecting data instead. I've stopped. Some of what I found changes the spec, so here it is briefly, followed by the plan and my questions.

Findings that affect the spec

  • The registered _r.xisf frames are not calibrated. Dust and hot pixels are fixed to the sensor, so calibration has to happen before alignment. The browser pipeline will be: raw crop → calibrate → align (warp) using the matrix in each .xdrz → stack. The _r files then serve as a check on our alignment code.
  • Meridian flip: frames 0–7 were taken on one side of the pier and 8–19 on the other, rotated about 180°. The largest same-side offset is frames 2/3 vs 5, about 47 px. Frame 3 has the satellite trail, so I'd use 2 and 5 on the Alignment page.
  • The synthetic FITS frames are stored upside-down compared with the raw XISF files, because FITS stores rows bottom-up. The precompute will flip them before applying their untouched relatives' alignment.
  • What each bad frame contains: frame 11 is the tracking error (trailed stars), and frame 3's satellite trail is faint, in the lower right. Both match your brief.
  • The master dark already contains the bias: its median is 161 against 160.5 for the bias. Dark current on this sensor is negligible, and the dark mostly adds hot pixels.
  • The old dark is from an ASI294MM Pro at 8288×5644, so its size doesn't match our sensor and it can't be subtracted directly.
  • Flat test on the dust mote: the 50% flat removes it cleanly, the 10% flat nearly does, and the 85% flat leaves it visible. That gives the Flats–Continued page real evidence.

Your plan, restated

  • What we're building: a desktop-only single-page app on Theme 1. It's a wizard that teaches calibration, then light-frame selection and stacking, using your real NGC 7331 data from Stella Venator Observatory. It ends in a workbench.
  • Teaching style: Park Tool. A short explanation, then a problem, then the user adjusts controls until the problem goes away, and can bring it back. Plain language throughout, with no "ADU" or "sigma".
  • Pages:
  • Welcome
  • Noise & Defects
  • Calibration: Bias, Darks, Flats, Flats–Continued
  • Alignment
  • Algorithms
  • Light Frames
  • Workbench
  • Workbench:
  • The user picks calibration frames first, then light frames. Each light frame shows its hardcoded histogram, FWHM and star count.
  • Algorithms: average, median, kappa-sigma, winsorized sigma, robust Chauvenet.
  • The user picks a reference frame. Four fixed ROIs update in under a second whenever a setting changes.
  • A full stack runs on request (4–10 s) and exports as FITS or PNG.
  • Scenario buttons: Default, Naive, Satellite, Cloud, Tracking.
  • Constraints:
  • All processing runs in the browser, with no backend.
  • Delivered as one Docker container on an Ubuntu VPS.
  • The browser back button keeps working.
  • Tailwind, Bauhaus style with a space theme that isn't too dark, fixed width, one or two columns.
  • Aim for a working POC in about 4 h and polish after that.
  • Phases:
  • Spec, plus data precompute in the background
  • Figma, starting with a design-philosophy discussion
  • Re-evaluate the spec against the design
  • M1: display and selection
  • M2: average and median, calibration, live ROIs
  • M3: lessons
  • M4: all algorithms and scenarios

Questions

Each has my recommendation. Reply with the numbers you disagree with.

  1. Full-image resolution. At full resolution, 24 frames take about 1.25 GB of browser memory and about 700 MB to download. That won't work in a browser tab, and the download is too slow for judges hitting a VPS. I recommend ROIs at native resolution, from small precomputed crops, and the full stack and export at 2×2 binning (3112×2084). The full frames would load only when someone asks for a full stack, roughly 200 MB. 3×3 binning is the fallback if that's too heavy.
  2. Getting the data to the VPS. The binned frames are too large for git. I recommend building the image here in WSL and pushing it to a container registry, or using docker save. We'd commit the regeneration script and the small assets, not the frame data. How do you plan to deploy?
  3. Bias and dark both selected. I recommend the correct behaviour: remove the bias from the dark first, so the light isn't bias-subtracted twice. Bias then only matters for flats when dark flats are off. The alternative is to let the user make the double-subtraction mistake on purpose.
  4. The old-camera dark. I recommend showing it only on the Darks page as an amp-glow example, not as a selectable option. It could be resampled to fit, but that looks fake.
  5. Normalization before stacking. Sky background varies between frames: medians range from 783 to 1062 raw brightness units (ADU, internal only). Without normalization, the rejection algorithms misbehave. I recommend always on, explained in one sentence, with no toggle.
  6. Changing the reference frame. I recommend that the stack re-aligns to the chosen frame and the ROIs follow the sky, so picking a post-flip frame shows the field rotated 180°.
  7. Cache. localStorage holds only about 5 MB and survives a refresh, and both conflict with your spec. I recommend an in-memory cache keyed by the exact settings. It clears on refresh automatically.
  8. ROI size. At native resolution the galaxy is about 2300×800 px, so a 512×512 ROI shows the core and the inner dust lanes but not the outer disk. What size do you want? My default is 512×512 for all four.
  9. Flat masters. I recommend precomputing all nine now: 10%, 50% and 85% exposures, each calibrated with dark flats, with bias, or with neither. The 10% and 85% sets would show up in the UI only on Flats–Continued.
  10. Start precompute now? Star metrics for 24 frames take about 20 minutes, and together with the flat masters and histograms they don't depend on the answers above. I recommend starting a background agent on them now while we finish the spec.
  11. Figma timebox. I suggest about 75 minutes: the shared library, one lesson-page template and the workbench in high fidelity, with the other pages at medium fidelity so their content is right.

Once you've answered, I'll write SPEC.md with the stories, file contracts and agent orchestration, then move on to the design-philosophy discussion.

# SPEC: Stacking Explainer (hackathon POC)

This is the source of truth for what we build and how agents build it. `AGENTS.md` covers repo conventions and tooling. `docs/knowledge/wbpp.md` covers the PixInsight WBPP pipeline that we replicate. When the three disagree, this file wins; fix the other two.

Status: **draft v1**. The spec is re-evaluated after Figma (phase 3). Decisions made with the product owner are logged in §12.

---

## 1. Product

An interactive, desktop-only lesson followed by a workbench. It teaches beginners how to choose **calibration frames** (bias, darks, flats, dark flats) and **light frames**, and how **stacking algorithms** deal with outliers. Everything runs on real data from **Stella Venator Observatory** (Lexington, Kentucky): NGC 7331, EdgeHD 11 at 2800 mm, AP26MC, Red filter, 20 × 300 s.

Contest theme 1, *Exploration & Understanding*. The judges score execution and polish, depth of knowledge, and creativity. One flow done well beats breadth.

**Teaching method (Park Tool style).** Every lesson step follows the same loop: explain the concept briefly → show a real problem in the data → the learner adjusts controls until the problem goes away → they can bring it back and fix it again. Every step has an interactive element with a tight feedback loop.

**Voice.** The prose sits between a textbook and an expert who is excited to share. Avoid short, pithy declarative sentences. The product owner edits all prose in Figma. See the plain-language rules in §9.

## 2. Scope

**In**
- Lesson pages: Welcome, Noise & Defects, Calibration (Bias, Darks, Flats, Flats–Continued), Alignment, Algorithms, Light Frames.
- Workbench: calibration choices, then frame selection with precomputed metrics, then algorithm and parameters, then reference frame, 4 fixed ROIs that update live, full-image stack on demand, and FITS/PNG export.
- Five scenario presets: Default, Naive, Satellite Trail Challenge, Cloud Challenge, Tracking Error Challenge.
- Pixel combination: average, median, kappa-sigma clipping, winsorized sigma clipping, robust Chauvenet rejection (RCR).
- Calibration in WBPP order, with every flat variant precomputed.
- One Docker container: a Node server that serves the SPA plus **one** ROI API endpoint.

**Out (cutting floor):** mobile, touch, Safari, accessibility, auth, persistence across refreshes, drizzle, colour or debayering, user-movable ROIs, computing registration ourselves (we use PixInsight's matrices), sky flats, and flat exposures other than the 10/50/85% sets. Also out, unless §6 finds WBPP depends on them: local normalization, cosmetic correction, subframe weighting.

## 3. Dataset

| Asset | Details |
|---|---|
| Lights | `source_images/light/*FRAME_00NN*.xisf`, NN = 00–19. 6224×4168 UInt16 mono, 300 s, gain 100, offset 160, about −4 °C. Frames 00–07 were shot with the telescope on the **West** side of the pier, 08–19 on the **East** side. The meridian flip rotates the image about 180°. |
| Defects | f03: real **satellite trail** (faint, lower right). f11: synthetic **tracking error** (trailed stars). f14–f16: synthetic **patchy cloud**. |
| Synthetic files | `source_images/light_synthetic_disaster/*.fits`. These are **vertically flipped** relative to the raw XISF (FITS stores rows bottom-up). Flip them once at conversion time. They use the alignment matrix of their untouched raw frame. |
| Registration | `light_registered/*_r.xdrz` `AlignmentMatrix` is a 3×3 homography that maps **reference coordinates (f07) → raw-frame coordinates**. The `_r.xisf` files are registered but **not calibrated**. We use them only as a test oracle for our warp. |
| Masters (from WBPP) | `masterBias` and `masterDark` (300 s) are Float32 in [0,1]; multiply by 65535 to get ADU. The master dark **includes the bias pedestal** (median ≈ 161 vs 160.5), so dark current is negligible and the dark mainly carries hot pixels. |
| Flats | Raw flats at 10% (0.11 s), 50% (2.24 s) and 85% (10 s) histogram levels, 25 each, plus matching dark flats. A quick test showed the 50% flat removes the left-side dust mote and the 85% flat does not. |
| Old-camera dark | `darkFromOlderCamera.fits`: ASI294MM Pro, 8288×5644, 600 s. **Display only** (amp-glow example). Never applied. |
| Final | `final/masterLight_*.xisf` (WBPP master, 6094×4092 autocrop) and `final/NGC7331.png` (colour composite). Used on the Welcome page. |

Pixel scale 0.277″/px. Registration offsets within one pier side are up to about 47 px (f02/f03 vs f05).

**Frame list (open question Q1, §11).** The recommendation is that learners see **20 frames**, with f11, f14, f15 and f16 shown as their synthetic defect versions. The clean originals are hidden so the same exposure is never counted twice.

## 4. Architecture

```
┌──────────────── Docker container (node:22-slim) ─────────────────┐
│ server/  Fastify                                                   │
│   GET /            → dist/ (built SPA, static)                     │
│   GET /data/*.json → precomputed JSON (static)                     │
│   GET /api/roi     → the ONE API: a pixel region of one asset      │
│ /data   baked in: raw pixel files + bin pyramid + JSON             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Browser: React + TS + Vite + Tailwind SPA. A Web Worker pool runs
         calibrate → warp → normalize → integrate. Nothing heavy runs
         on the server.
```

- **Frontend:** React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind v4, `react-router` with `HashRouter`, and zustand for state. React plus Tailwind matches the Figma MCP's code output. Charts and diagrams are hand-written SVG components with no chart library.
- **Server:** Node 22 and Fastify with `@fastify/static`. It has no processing logic beyond 2×2 binning of the requested region.
- **Orientation:** every image is shown in **canonical orientation**, which is the West-side sensor orientation (f07). East-side frames and stacks are rotated 180° for display. Calibration frames are sensor-space, which is already canonical.

### 4.1 Coordinate spaces (contract)
- **Sensor space of asset A:** pixel column x (rightwards) and row y (downwards). Row 0 is the first row of the XISF array. Calibration happens here.
- **Canonical space:** f07's sensor grid, which is the PixInsight registration reference. ROI definitions live here at bin 1.
- `H_i`: the 3×3 matrix taken from the xdrz. It maps canonical to frame i's sensor space. The **pixel-origin convention** (matrix applied to pixel centres at +0.5 or at integers) is fixed by `data/derived/precompute/geometry_check.json` (Stage A) and must be quoted in `src/shared/pipeline/geometry.ts`.
- **Output grid for reference r:** M_{out→i} = H_i · H_r⁻¹ · F_r, where F_r is the identity for West frames and a 180° rotation about the image centre for East frames. The stack is aligned to r's pixel grid but keeps the canonical orientation.
- **Binning b ∈ {1,2,4,8}:** conjugate the matrices with the bin scale under the same origin convention. The pipeline tests cover b = 1 against PixInsight's `_r.xisf` and b = 2 for consistency with b = 1.

### 4.2 Runtime data (`/data`, produced by `tools/precompute`, git-ignored, baked into the image)
- `manifest.json` lists every asset: id, kind (`light` | `master` | `flat` | `darkflat`), width, height, dtype, per-bin file paths, and for lights also pier side, defect, relative, header fields and `H` (9 floats).
- Pixel files: raw little-endian, row-major, no header.
  - Lights at b1 are `u16`. Masters are `f32` **in ADU**.
  - Bins 2, 4 and 8 are precomputed `f32` means. The server never bins a whole frame at request time.
  - Synthetic frames are stored already flipped.
- Precomputed JSON: `stars.json`, `histograms.json`, `normalization.json` (per frame × calibration combination; §6), and `calibration.json` (per-master statistics and STF parameters).
- Asset ids: lights `f00`…`f19`, `f11_tracking`, `f14_cloud`, `f15_cloud`, `f16_cloud`. Masters `bias`, `dark`, `darkflat_{10,50,85}`, and `flat_{10,50,85}_{darkflat,bias,none}` (9 master flats; the suffix is how the flat was calibrated).

### 4.3 ROI API (the one endpoint)
`GET /api/roi?id=<assetId>&x=<int>&y=<int>&w=<int>&h=<int>&bin=<1|2|4|8>`
- x, y, w and h are in the asset's own **sensor space at bin 1**. For bin > 1 they must be multiples of `bin`, and the response holds (w/bin)×(h/bin) samples.
- The rectangle is clamped to the image. Response headers are `X-Roi: x,y,w,h` (the clamped rectangle, bin-1 units), `X-Width`, `X-Height` (sample dimensions) and `X-Dtype: u16|f32`. The body is raw little-endian samples, row-major.
- Limits: at most 8 MP per request, unknown id → 404, bad rectangle → 400. Reads use positioned `fs.read` per row; whole files are never loaded. `Cache-Control: no-store`.

### 4.4 Client pipeline (`src/shared/pipeline`, pure TS, runs in workers)
`stack(req: StackRequest) → StackResult`
```ts
type StackRequest = {
  grid: { ref: FrameId; x: number; y: number; w: number; h: number; bin: 1|2|4|8 }; // canonical-oriented output rect
  frames: FrameId[];                 // order-insensitive
  calibration: CalibrationChoice;    // §6
  algorithm: { name: 'average'|'median'|'kappaSigma'|'winsorized'|'rcr'; params?: Record<string, number> };
  align?: boolean;                   // default true; false = naive stack (Alignment lesson)
};
type StackResult = { data: Float32Array; w: number; h: number; rejectedLow: Uint8Array; rejectedHigh: Uint8Array; noise: number; ms: number };
```
Per frame: **footprint** (map the output rectangle through M, pad by the interpolation radius, clamp) → **fetch** light and master crops for that sensor rectangle at the same bin → **calibrate** in sensor space (§6) → **warp** with PixInsight-equivalent interpolation (§6); pixels outside the frame become NaN and are excluded → **normalize** with precomputed coefficients (§6). Then, per output pixel over the finite samples: **integrate** with the chosen algorithm, keeping per-pixel rejection counts.

- **Performance budget:** 4 workbench ROIs at bin 2 with 20 frames in **< 1 s** total on a desktop. A full stack at bin 1 is processed in bands of about 256 rows, spread across `hardwareConcurrency − 1` workers, with progress reporting and cancel. Peak memory stays under 1.5 GB.
- **Fetch cache:** in memory, keyed by (id, rect, bin), with a byte-capped LRU.
- **Result cache:** in memory, keyed by the canonical JSON of `StackRequest` (frames sorted), with a byte-capped LRU. It clears on refresh. No localStorage.

### 4.5 Display
- **Lights and stacks:** PixInsight AutoSTF (target background 0.25, shadows clip −2.8·MADN, linked). The parameters come from the **reference frame's** precomputed median and MADN for the active calibration combination, so every view in that state shares one stretch. The JS STF must match `tools/astro.py` (unit-tested against Python output).
- **Bias, dark, dark flat:** each uses its own AutoSTF.
- **Flats:** linear, no stretch. Map the 0.1–99.9 percentile range to display range.
- **Reference view:** the reference frame at bin 4, calibrated, with markers for the 4 ROIs.
- **ROI tiles:** the workbench shows ROIs of different sizes in one normalized tile form factor (layout set in Figma) with a scale indicator.
- **Noise readout (per ROI):** robust standard deviation (MADN) of the ROI's background pixels after clipping stars, in reference-normalized units, plus the ratio to a single reference frame (for example "3.9× less noise than one frame"). How SNR is presented is decided in Figma.

### 4.6 Routing, state, export
- **Hash routes**, one history entry per page: `#/welcome`, `#/noise`, `#/calibration/{bias,darks,flats,flats-2}`, `#/alignment`, `#/algorithms`, `#/light-frames`, `#/workbench`. The back and forward buttons work.
- **Sections** live in `src/sections/<name>/` and register through one list, `src/shell/sections.ts`, one line each. Shared code lives in `src/shared/` and has one owner.
- **Export** (full stack only):
  - FITS: float32 BITPIX −32, linear, [0,1]. Header: `IMAGETYP='Master Light'`, `NCOMBINE`, `EXPTIME`, `TOTEXP`, `REFFRAME`, `CALIB`, `ALGO` and parameters, `SOFTWARE`.
  - PNG: 8-bit with the current stretch.
  - The filename encodes the settings.

### 4.7 Build and run
- `npm run dev` runs Vite and the server together, with `/api` proxied. `npm run build`, `npm test` (vitest), `npm run e2e` (Playwright, Chromium + Firefox), `uv run pytest tools`.
- `docker build -t stacking-explainer .` then `docker run -p 8080:8080 stacking-explainer`. The build is multi-stage (build the SPA, then a slim runtime). `.dockerignore` excludes `source_images/`, `.venv`, `node_modules`, and everything under `data/` except `data/derived/runtime`. The product owner handles `docker save` and the VPS.

## 5. Precompute (Python, `tools/precompute/`, outputs in `data/derived/`)

| Stage | Output | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| A | `frames.json`, `geometry_check.json` (matrix direction, pixel origin, synthetic flip), `stars.json` + `stars/<id>.csv`, `histograms.json` | none (running) |
| B | 3 master dark flats, 9 master flats (WBPP method); `normalization.json` per frame × calibration combination; `calibration.json` (master statistics and STF) | `docs/knowledge/wbpp.md` |
| C | `runtime/`: pixel files (b1 plus the b2/b4/b8 pyramid) and `manifest.json` | Stage B and §4.2 |
| D | Static art: Welcome images (stretched single sub, stretched WBPP master, resized colour composite), the old-camera amp-glow image, Alignment star trio, golden test fixtures (§10) | Figma sizes |

Every stage has one `run_stage_<x>.sh` so it can be regenerated, as AGENTS.md requires.

## 6. Processing semantics (WBPP-faithful)

> **Pending `docs/knowledge/wbpp.md`.** This section is filled from the research. It will pin: the light calibration formula and bias/dark toggle semantics, master flat construction and how the flat is normalized, normalization (estimators, reference, what is precomputed), interpolation (StarAlignment default), each algorithm's exact maths and defaults, which parameters are exposed, out-of-frame and zero-pixel handling, and weighting.

`CalibrationChoice` (UI order: bias → dark → flat):
```ts
type CalibrationChoice = { bias: boolean; dark: boolean; flat: null | { level: 10|50|85; flatCal: 'darkflat'|'bias'|'none' } };
```
That gives 2 × 2 × 10 = 40 combinations. `normalization.json` holds the per-frame location and scale for each combination.

## 7. Pages

Each page lists its goal, its problem → fix interaction, the data it uses, and acceptance criteria (AC). Layout, prose and art come from Figma. The ROI sizes and positions below are **placeholders until Figma**.

**P0 Welcome.** The emotional hook: one 300 s sub → WBPP master → final colour image, with a clear line that these are real images from Stella Venator Observatory in Lexington, KY. Data: Stage D static images. AC: renders in under 2 s on localhost; Start goes to `#/noise`.

**P1 Noise & Defects.** What makes up a light frame: target and sky signal, random noise, bias offset, dark signal and hot pixels, uneven response (vignetting, dust), and non-hardware problems (clouds, tracking, satellites, planes). Also why we stack, and what "calibration frames" means. Interactive: the **system SVG** (telescope → camera → sensor → sensor PCB with op-amp and ADC) with colour-coded noise layers. Selecting a layer highlights where it comes from. Also a "why stack" control that averages 1 → N frames on a background ROI to show noise falling. AC: every layer is selectable, and the N-frame noise readout falls roughly as 1/√N.

**P2 Bias.** Problem: every pixel sits on an offset added by the readout electronics. Fix: subtract the bias. Interactive: a bias toggle on a light ROI, with its histogram and a sample pixel's brightness moving (for example about 1,060 → 900). The master bias is shown with its own stretch, and the op-amp/ADC layer peels away in the SVG. AC: the histogram shift equals the master bias median to within 1 ADU.

**P3 Darks.** Problem: hot pixels (and amp glow on some cameras). Fix: subtract a dark taken at the same exposure time and temperature as the lights. Interactive: an ROI rich in hot pixels, toggling none → bias only → dark. The old-camera dark is shown only to illustrate amp glow. The page notes that this dark was taken at a slightly different temperature, which is acceptable here, and that on this camera the dark is mostly bias plus hot pixels. AC: visible hot pixels disappear only with the dark applied.

**P4 Flats.** Problem: vignetting and dust shadows. Fix: divide by a flat, and calibrate that flat with dark flats. Interactive: a dust-mote ROI and a bin-8 full-field view; toggle the flat, then toggle how the flat itself was calibrated (dark flats / bias / none) to show what an uncalibrated flat does. AC: the mote and vignetting vanish with the 50% flat calibrated by dark flats.

**P5 Flats–Continued.** Why the histogram target matters. Interactive: choose the 10%, 50% or 85% flat, see each flat's histogram, and see the dust-mote ROI corrected with each. An optional aside on full-well depth is the product owner's call. AC: the result for each level matches Stage B.

**P6 Alignment.** How frames are brought together and why that raises SNR. Interactive: f02 + f05 (about 47 px apart, same pier side) averaged **without alignment**, which doubles the stars. The trio of stars used for alignment is highlighted, with offset vectors taken from the Stage A catalogues. Toggle align and the stars merge. Then attention turns to the **background**, where the noise readout shows about a 1/√2 drop. AC: the naive stack clearly shows doubled stars; the aligned stack matches the pipeline golden output.

**P7 Algorithms.** How each algorithm decides what an outlier is, explained with high-school maths ("standard deviation", never "sigma"). Interactive: a 5-frame stack that includes f03, shown with average and median side by side on the satellite ROI. There is guidance on which algorithm suits which frame count (from §6). *Proposal A (§11):* a pixel-stack inspector. AC: the trail is visible with average and gone with median.

**P8 Light Frames.** Choosing good frames. FWHM, star counts and histograms are tools, and judgement still matters. A lighter version of the workbench: every frame with its thumbnail, metrics and histogram; average or median; one galaxy ROI; full calibration applied and locked; a teaser for the other algorithms. AC: selection changes update the ROI in under 1 s.

**P9 Workbench.** Layout is designed together in Figma. Order of interaction:
1. Calibration panel (bias, dark, flat level and flat calibration). Selecting a calibration frame shows it with the correct stretch.
2. Frame list (20 entries, each with metrics and a histogram; select or deselect; set as reference).
3. Algorithm and parameters.
4. Scenario buttons.
5. Reference view with the 4 ROI markers, and the ROI tiles updating live at bin 2.
6. **Stack full image** (bin 1, progress, cancel), then the result view, then export as FITS or PNG.

Default ROIs, in canonical space, with positions and sizes set in Figma: (1) the satellite trail in f03, (2) the central galaxy including faint outer structure, (3) the galaxy group just above it, (4) the dust mote on the left.
*Teaching note:* the dust mote and hot pixels are fixed to the **sensor**. Because of the meridian flip, East-side frames place the mote at the opposite side of the sky. In a stack the mote only comes from the West frames, which is why median and rejection weaken it even without flats.

**Scenarios** (defined in `src/sections/workbench/scenarios.ts`):

| Scenario | Frames | Algorithm | Calibration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Default | All frames without a synthetic defect (f03 is included) | median | full (per §6) |
| Naive | All 20 | average | full |
| Satellite Trail Challenge | f03 + 4 clean frames from the same side | average | full |
| Cloud Challenge | f14–f16 (cloud) + the 2 best frames by FWHM and star count | average | full |
| Tracking Error Challenge | f11 (tracking) + the 2 best frames | average | full |

AC: each button sets the full state in one click, and the ROIs update in under 1 s.

## 8. Milestones and stories

Gates for every merge to `main`: `uv run pytest tools`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run build`. At the end of each milestone, add `npm run e2e` (smoke) and a `docker build` plus container smoke test (`/` and one `/api/roi`).

**Phase 1 (now):** this spec, WBPP knowledge, precompute stages A and B.
**Phase 2:** Figma (library plus one page per section), with the product owner.
**Phase 3:** re-evaluate this spec against the design and update §7 and §11.

**M1: display and selection**
- M1-01 Scaffold: Vite/React/TS/Tailwind, Fastify server, Dockerfile, npm scripts, vitest, Playwright, section registry, and design tokens taken from the Figma library.
- M1-02 Runtime data (Stage C) and the ROI API with unit tests (clamping, binning, dtype, limits).
- M1-03 Data client (typed fetch, fetch cache) and the JS STF, tested against Python.
- M1-04 App shell: wizard navigation (previous, next, progress), hash routing, back button.
- M1-05 Workbench shell: every control present. Frame list with metrics and histograms. Calibration frame viewer with the correct stretch. Reference view with ROI markers. ROI tiles that show crops of the reference frame as placeholders.
- M1-06 Skeletons for every lesson page, using the Figma layouts with placeholder content.
- AC: click through every light and calibration frame with the correct stretch and orientation; back button works; `docker run` serves the app.

**M2: average and median, calibration, live ROIs**
- M2-01 Pipeline core: footprint, calibrate, warp, normalize, average and median, NaN edges, worker pool.
- M2-02 Golden tests: a numpy reference implementation of `stack()` for small ROIs, with fixtures compared in vitest within tolerance. Warp checked against PixInsight `_r.xisf` at b1.
- M2-03 Live ROIs (4 × bin 2 in under 1 s), result cache, noise readout.
- M2-04 Full stack: band streaming, progress, cancel, result view, FITS and PNG export.
- AC: calibration is applied in WBPP order, and the ROIs update on every change.

**M3: lessons.** Each page's interactive element and Figma prose, per §7.
**M4: all algorithms and scenarios.** Kappa-sigma, winsorized and RCR with their exposed parameters; the five scenarios.
**Polish:** whatever is left of the 8 hours.

## 9. Language rules for prose and UI copy
- Say "pixel brightness", not ADU. Say "standard deviation", not sigma. Say "dark frames taken with the same exposure time and temperature as your lights", not "matched darks".
- Define every term the first time it appears: light, bias, dark, flat, dark flat, stack, master, reference frame.
- No asides that don't serve the current step. One idea per paragraph.

## 10. Orchestration (autonomous implementation and validation)

**Ownership and models**

| Role | Model / effort | Owns |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator (main session) | Opus, high | SPEC.md, AGENTS.md, contracts (§4.1–4.4 types), merges to `main`, gates, reviews |
| Foundation | Opus, high | M1-01, M1-04, `src/shared/` UI primitives and tokens. **Lands first**; everyone else branches from it. |
| Data + server | Sonnet, medium | `tools/precompute/` stages B–D, `server/`, M1-02 |
| Pipeline | Opus, high | `src/shared/pipeline/`, golden fixtures, M2-01/02/04, M4 algorithms |
| Workbench UI | Sonnet, medium | `src/sections/workbench/`, M1-05, M2-03 integration, scenarios |
| Lesson UI (2–3 agents) | Sonnet, medium | `src/sections/<page>/`, split by page group: [welcome, noise], [bias, darks, flats, flats-2], [alignment, algorithms, light-frames] |
| Validator | Sonnet, medium | Runs gates and Playwright screenshot tours after every merge, compares them with the Figma frames, files issues in `TODO.md` |

**Rules**
- Code agents run in git worktrees on `section/<name>`, `asset/<name>` or `core/<name>`. Worktrees don't contain `source_images/` or `data/`, so they read runtime data through `ASTRO_DATA=<abs path to main>/data/derived/runtime`.
- An agent receives this spec, its section brief and the contracts, not the chat history. An agent touches only the files it owns. A cross-boundary change becomes a request in `TODO.md`.
- Agents rebase onto `main` and run the gates. The orchestrator merges. Commit messages follow AGENTS.md.
- **Waves:** (0) precompute and research → (1) Foundation alone → (2) Data+server, Pipeline, Workbench UI and Lesson skeletons in parallel → (3) M2 integration → (4) M3 lessons ‖ M4 algorithms → polish.

## 11. Open questions, proposals, risks

**Questions for the product owner**
- Q1: 20 frames with defects replacing their originals (recommended), or all 24 entries?

**Deferred to Figma:** ROI sizes and positions, the normalized ROI tile form factor, page layouts, SVG art direction, and all prose.

**Proposals (not in scope unless approved):**
- A. Pixel-stack inspector on P7: click a pixel to see its N values as dots and which ones each algorithm rejects. It is the most direct way to show how an outlier is chosen.
- B. Rejection-map overlay on the workbench ROIs. The data comes free from the integration loop.
- C. Live full-field stack at bin 8 in the reference view.

**Risks**
- A full-resolution stack pulls about 1.0 GB of lights plus the master crops from the server. That is fast on localhost or a LAN and takes minutes over the internet.
- The satellite trail is faint. In a 5-frame average it may be hard to see, so check in M2 and adjust the Satellite scenario's frame count.
- Lanczos warping cost in JS. There is a budget in §4.4, and the fallback is a cheaper kernel, noted in §6.

## 12. Decision log
- 2026-09-24:
  - Lessons use native-resolution ROIs only. Workbench ROIs are 2×2 binned. The full stack runs at full resolution. Source images are never down-binned for delivery.
  - One backend endpoint (ROI regions) is authorized.
  - Deployment is via `docker save`, owned by the product owner.
  - The old-camera dark is display-only.
  - Normalization is authorized and precomputed.
  - Changing the reference re-registers the stack to it, and images keep one canonical orientation.
  - Cache is in memory only and clears on refresh.
  - ROI sizes are deferred to Figma.
  - All 9 flat masters are precomputed.
  - Figma timeboxing is handled by the product owner with the design agent.
  - Masters must follow PixInsight WBPP (knowledge in `docs/knowledge/wbpp.md`).

WBPP research and Stage-A precompute are both running in the background. While they work, I've drafted the spec.

Done so far - SPEC.md (draft v1) covers the product, scope, dataset facts, architecture and contracts. The contracts are the coordinate spaces, the single /api/roi endpoint, the runtime data format and the stack() interface. It also has the precompute stages, the page-by-page interactions with acceptance criteria, milestones M1–M4 as stories, agent orchestration, and a log of your decisions from this round. - §6 (processing semantics) is a placeholder until the WBPP research lands. That research will settle the bias/dark toggle behaviour, how master flats are built, the normalization estimators, the rejection defaults and the interpolation method. - AGENTS.md now points to SPEC.md and describes the one-endpoint server. It also lists the dataset quirks every agent must know and links the new WBPP knowledge file.

Three calls I made that you may want to override - Frontend is React + TS + Vite + Tailwind, because the Figma MCP produces React + Tailwind code. - "Same orientation": East-side frames and stacks are rotated 180° for display, so switching the reference never turns the view upside-down. - Per-ROI noise readout: it's in scope, e.g. "3.9× less noise than one frame". It's the most direct feedback for "highest SNR". How SNR is presented is left for Figma.

One question while the agents run

Q1: Should learners see 20 frames, with the four defect versions (f11 tracking, f14–16 cloud) replacing their clean originals? Or all 24 entries? I recommend 20, so the same exposure is never stacked twice.

§11 also has three optional additions for later: a pixel-stack inspector on the Algorithms page, a rejection-map overlay, and a live full-field overview.

When the research finishes, I'll fill in §6, start the Stage-B precompute (master flats and normalization), and send you the finished spec for review.
